name: Protein-heavy growth diet

card.summary: Eating enough protein and calories in puberty supports growth; surplus protein is untested for extra height.
card.note: Nutrition matters when deficient; no evidence of gains beyond genetic potential.

quick.overview:
The diet idea is to eat enough protein and calories during puberty so nutrition does not limit growth.

Undernutrition is documented to reduce adult height, but studies of extra protein in well-nourished teens were not found.
quick.mechanism: Growth depends on adequate energy and amino acids alongside genetics and hormones. Population data link protein-rich diets with taller average stature.
quick.risks: A balanced diet is ordinary; individuals with kidney or metabolic conditions follow medical guidance on protein. Extreme diets carry their own nutritional risks.

lead: A protein-heavy growth diet is an approach discussed in height communities in which adolescents eat adequate or high amounts of protein and calories, often from meat, dairy and eggs, so that nutrition does not limit growth and they reach their full genetic height. Unlike many height claims, it relates to a documented determinant of growth: childhood nutrition [1].

Reference sources describe adult height as 60 to 80 percent heritable and state that chronic malnutrition in childhood and adolescence can delay growth and reduce adult height [1]. National average height is described as correlating with protein quality, with countries eating more meat, dairy, eggs and fish tending to be taller [1]. A study of Guatemalan Maya children found those raised in the United States about 10 cm taller than peers in Guatemala, attributed largely to better nutrition and health care [1].

Children need more protein than adults because it supports growth and development [2]. Sources do not report that eating more protein than needed in an already well-nourished adolescent increases height beyond genetic potential.

chain: Adequate protein and calories during puberty
Growth is not limited by nutrition
angle.text: Teenagers and parents use a protein- and calorie-sufficient diet so that growth has the building blocks it needs. The aim is to avoid losing height to undernutrition, not to exceed genetic potential.

infobox: About 0.8 g/kg body weight; children need more [2]

paras: Proponents encourage sufficient calories and protein-rich foods during puberty so nutrition is not a limiting factor. Some also discuss calcium and vitamin D. Protein comes from animal sources such as meat, dairy, eggs and fish and from plant sources such as legumes, nuts and whole grains [2].

Childhood and adolescence are described as critical periods in which undernutrition can reduce adult height even without a medical condition [1]. Population comparisons link taller average stature with diets richer in animal protein, though differences between populations may reflect genetics, lifestyle or both [1]. Growth is described as ending on average around age 15 or 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males [1]. Severe protein-energy malnutrition is linked with failure to grow and with kwashiorkor [2].

Health authorities have not set a tolerable upper limit for protein. Surplus amino acids are broken down in the liver and excreted as urea, excess protein may raise urinary calcium and possibly kidney stone risk, and people with chronic kidney disease are advised to limit protein [2].

No studies found testing a protein-heavy diet specifically as a height-maximising protocol in well-nourished adolescents. Population and malnutrition research, summarised in reference works, links poor childhood nutrition with reduced adult height [1].

lore.intro: In height forums, adequate nutrition is often described as a lever for teenagers, in contrast with supplements or devices.

claims.claim: Eating enough protein and calories lets you reach your full genetic height.
claims.believers: Proponents point to taller populations with high animal-protein intake and to teens who grew after improving their diet.
claims.experts: Reference sources report that chronic malnutrition reduces adult height and that protein quality correlates with population height; they do not report extra height from surplus protein in well-nourished youth [1].

claims.claim: Extra protein beyond normal needs adds height.
claims.believers: Some posters advocate very high protein intake during puberty to maximise growth.
claims.experts: No published study was found testing very high protein intake for increased height in well-nourished adolescents.
